## One step up the page, one letter up the alphabet

Move a note head up one position on the staff and its letter advances by one.
That part is easy. What the page won't tell you is whether the pitch rose by one
semitone or by two. Printed notation counts in letters, MIDI counts in
semitones, and the two run at different rates. Treat one visual step as one MIDI
step and you'll be wrong on a third of your notes.

The *staff* is five lines and the four spaces between them. A *treble clef*
fixes G4 on the second line from the bottom, and every other letter follows from
that anchor around the repeating A-to-G cycle. Middle C hangs below the staff on
a short ledger line of its own. Call it coordinate 0, count one per line-or-space
step, and the bottom line E4 lands on 2, with D4 in the space below at 1.

## The staff, drawn in characters

Here's the coordinate space as a table you can read down. Every number agrees
with what `staff_record` computes below.

```text
coord  note  midi   treble staff
  11    G5    79                          space above the staff
  10    F5    77    ------------------    fifth line
   9    E5    76                          fourth space
   8    D5    74    ------------------    fourth line
   7    C5    72                          third space
   6    B4    71    ------------------    third line
   5    A4    69                          second space
   4    G4    67    ------------------    second line, the clef's G
   3    F4    65                          first space
   2    E4    64    ------------------    first line
   1    D4    62                          space below the staff
   0    C4    60         ---------        middle C, its own ledger line
  -1    B3    59
  -2    A3    57         ---------        second ledger line
```

Engraved staff figures are still to come in this book. Read the sketch above as
scaffolding, never as a replacement for real notation.

Watch the two left columns drift apart. Coordinates step by one every time.
MIDI steps by one from E4 to F4 and from B4 to C5, and by two everywhere else.

## Eight positions in a row

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 90
use_synth :piano

letters = [:c, :d, :e, :f, :g, :a, :b]
semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}

define :staff_record do |position, letters, semitones|
  letter = letters[position % 7]
  octave = 4 + (position / 7).floor
  midi = 12 * (octave + 1) + semitones[letter]
  {position: position, letter: letter, octave: octave, midi: midi}
end

# Eight printed positions: bottom line through the space above the staff.
printed_positions = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]

printed_positions.each do |position|
  record = staff_record(position, letters, semitones)
  puts "position #{position}: #{record[:letter]}#{record[:octave]} midi=#{record[:midi]}"
  play record[:midi], release: 0.55
  sleep 0.75
end

# One-octave cheat sheet from middle C to the next C.
(0..7).each { |position| puts staff_record(position, letters, semitones) }
```

Eight even steps up the page, E4 through E5, one letter at a time. Your ear
hears something less even. Positions 2 and 3 sit one step apart, and so do 3
and 4. Which pair sounds wider to you?

Sing them back before reading on. The log answers it in the MIDI column, but
your ear gets there first.

## Change the list, not the function

1. Replace the list with `[0, 2, 4, 6]`. Skipping every other position from
   middle C picks out C4, E4, G4, and B4. Regular visual skips, and they spell a
   C major seventh chord.
2. Alternate positions `2` and `3`, then `3` and `4`. E to F is one staff step
   and one semitone; F to G is the same step on the page and twice the distance
   in the air.
3. Add positions `-1` and `-2` from the foot of the diagram. Ruby's modulo and
   floor division carry the letter and octave cycles below middle C without a
   second lookup table.

## Two counters, one conversion

Seven letter names form a ring. Position modulo seven picks the letter, floor
division counts completed trips around it and bumps the octave, and only then
does the `semitones` hash turn a name into a chromatic distance. Diatonic first,
chromatic second. The two spaces stay separate in the code because they measure
different things.

Treble clef is an offset convention. Nail one known pitch to one line and the
rest of the page follows. Line and space mnemonics give you quick spot checks,
but they split one system into two memorised lists and stop working the moment a
melody leaves the five lines. Coordinates handle all three cases alike.

[Lesson 40](40-key-signatures-defaults.qmd) lets accidentals and key signatures change the chromatic result
without moving the note head. F and F-sharp share coordinate 3, because both are
still the letter F; the sharp arrives later, in the semitone lookup. That's one
more reason not to read MIDI distance off vertical spacing.

Real notation carries time too, through stems, beams, rests, and dots. None of
it is here, deliberately, so vertical position is the only field that changes.
[Lesson 41](41-decode-four-printed-bars.qmd) hands rhythm back in a separate `:duration` key.

## Build the card you'd tape to the monitor

Generate a Markdown table for coordinates `-2` through `10`: the coordinate, whether
it's a line or a space, the letter, the octave, the Sonic Pi symbol, and the MIDI
integer. Mark middle C at coordinate 0 and mark the five treble lines. Print it.
You'll want it for the rest of Part 8.

Then pick eight note heads from a printed source, type in their coordinates, and
play the sequence without copying note names from anyone else's transcription.
Check coordinates against the page, conversion against the log. They catch
different mistakes.
